content.title: From Moanalua to Mission Control: Meet the Hawaii scientist keeping Artemis II on track
content.text: HONOLULU (HawaiiNewsNow) - While many watched the launch of NASA’s Artemis II mission in awe, Angela Garcia had a different vantage point as a NASA science officer supporting the agency’s return to deep-space exploration.“There (were) a few pinch, like, pinch myself in these real moments,” she said.The 2013 Moanalua High School graduate is based at NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston, where she works as a planetary exploration geologist.“It’s a new discipline that got integrated into the flight operations directorate,” Garcia said, noting that during the mission, she ensures “lunar science is getting advocated for in that room, and is getting accomplished during the mission.”Garcia and other scientists work closely with the astronauts, who collect observations and imagery that can later be analyzed by teams on the ground. She said much of the mission’s scientific value comes from visual documentation.“You are collecting all that data so that the scientists on Earth can interpret what you mean and try to hypothesize why you are seeing the things that you are seeing,” she said. “They’re taking images of the moon, of the Earth, of the solar corona, during the flyby. We’re looking at those images.”Garcia says her Hawaii upbringing paved her road to NASA. Time spent outdoors, trips to neighbor islands, and ocean swims all fueled a lifelong curiosity about the natural world.“Hawaii is very special in that way, that it makes you really face nature, and you have to respect it,” she said. “And so just applying that to the ultimate, I think, most humbling type of place you could go, which is into the vacuum of space, and trying to understand how to live among that, how to study it, how to really survive.” She also credited her success to mentors at Moanalua High School, singling out science teacher Erron Yoshioka, whom she calls “Yosh.”“He was just such a stable presence for everybody there in such a turbulent time, which is high school,” Garcia said. “I can’t thank Yosh enough for being able to show us beauty in nature and guide us along the way, so shout out to him for instilling so much love in all of us.”Yoshioka said, “I am so proud for her to be doing something so exciting, special, and groundbreaking. I know she is now an inspiration to so many of our local kids to ‘shoot for the moon and beyond.’”Family support has also been central to her journey. Her sister, Nadia Garcia Holt, said, “How proud am I that my little sister is on the team, spearheading the collective recognition of our place in the cosmos, not just Hawaii’s place, but the Earth, and all the places we can go. It brings tears to my eyes and joy.”Garcia said that support is something she’ll carry with her into future Artemis missions.Copyright 2026 Hawaii News Now. All rights reserved.
